note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/13 An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry/13.1 Formulas, functional groups and the naming of organic compounds.md
outline: A hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen only; alkanes are simple hydrocarbons with no functional group. Functional groups govern characteristic properties. General formulas describe series; structural formulas show connectivity, displayed formulas show all bonds, and skeletal formulas omit carbon labels and carbon-bound hydrogen. Name an aliphatic compound from its parent chain, functional-group suffix and lowest locants; for an ester name the O-bound alkyl group first. Count atoms for molecular formula and reduce subscripts for empirical formula.

misconceptions.statement: An alkane has a functional group because it contains C–H bonds.
misconceptions.refutation: Alkanes are hydrocarbons with no functional group; the C–H and C–C bonds do not define a functional group.
misconceptions.contrast: Identify a characteristic reactive grouping beyond the alkane framework.

misconceptions.statement: All compounds with the same molecular formula have the same properties.
misconceptions.refutation: The functional group determines characteristic chemical behaviour and strongly influences physical properties.
misconceptions.contrast: Identify the functional group, not just the atom totals.

misconceptions.statement: Every carbon and hydrogen is written explicitly in a skeletal formula.
misconceptions.refutation: Unlabelled vertices and line ends represent carbon; hydrogens attached to carbon are omitted and inferred from valency four.
misconceptions.contrast: Count vertices and ends, then complete carbon valencies.

misconceptions.statement: Name an ester from the carbon chain attached to oxygen first.
misconceptions.refutation: In an ester RCOOR′, name the alkyl group R′ first, then the carboxylate RCOO second.
misconceptions.contrast: Identify the C–O–C(=O) boundary before naming.

misconceptions.statement: An empirical formula is necessarily the molecular formula.
misconceptions.refutation: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio; the molecular formula gives actual numbers of atoms.
misconceptions.contrast: Reduce molecular subscripts only when asked for empirical formula.

misconceptions.statement: Containing some carbon and hydrogen is sufficient to be a hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.refutation: Every atom must be carbon or hydrogen; any other element excludes membership.
misconceptions.contrast: Check the complete element list, not just the first two symbols.

misconceptions.statement: Every organic compound must possess a functional group.
misconceptions.refutation: Alkanes are organic hydrocarbons with no functional group.
misconceptions.contrast: An alkene has a carbon–carbon double bond; an alkane framework alone has no functional group.

misconceptions.statement: Any carbonyl-containing compound is a ketone.
misconceptions.refutation: Inspect what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon: hydrogen, two carbons, hydroxyl or an oxygen-linked carbon distinguishes classes.
misconceptions.contrast: An ester and an aldehyde contain carbonyl bonds but are not ketones.

misconceptions.statement: The nitrile carbon is excluded from the parent chain.
misconceptions.refutation: Include the carbon of the nitrile group in the parent chain and number it carbon 1.
misconceptions.contrast: An alkyl fragment with two carbons gives a three-carbon nitrile.

misconceptions.statement: The ester alkyl part includes the carbonyl carbon.
misconceptions.refutation: Only the group beyond the single-bond oxygen supplies the alkyl name; the carbonyl carbon belongs to the acid-derived chain.
misconceptions.contrast: Separate the two sides at the single-bond oxygen before counting.
misconceptions.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf p.12; ER 9701 s19 P22 Q5

steps.why: It separates acid-derived and alcohol-derived parts.

items.stem: Four compounds are listed: ethane, but-1-ene, cyclohexane and ethanol. Identify the compound that is not a hydrocarbon, with the correct reason.

options.A: Ethanol, because it contains oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen.
options.B: But-1-ene, because its C=C bond is a functional group.
options.C: Cyclohexane, because its carbon atoms form a ring and not a chain.
options.D: Ethane, because its C-H bonds act as a functional group.

items.explanation: A hydrocarbon is a compound made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms only. Ethanol, $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$, also contains oxygen, so it is not a hydrocarbon. But-1-ene and cyclohexane contain only carbon and hydrogen, whatever their bonding or shape, and the C-H bonds of ethane are not a functional group.

Check which elements each compound contains, not how its carbon atoms are bonded.

items.stem: Propane, $\ce{C3H8}$, is a member of the alkanes. Which statement about functional groups in propane is correct?

options.A: Propane has no functional group; its C-C and C-H bonds do not make one.
options.B: Propane has a functional group because it contains C-H bonds.
options.C: Propane has a $\ce{-CH3}$ functional group at each end of the chain.
options.D: Propane has a functional group because every one of its carbon atoms is saturated.

items.explanation: Alkanes are simple saturated hydrocarbons with no functional group: a functional group is a reactive grouping beyond the alkane framework of C-C and C-H single bonds. The claims that C-H bonds or terminal methyl groups are functional groups mistake part of that framework for a functional group, and being saturated is the absence of a reactive grouping, not the presence of one.
hints: Recall how the syllabus describes the alkanes.
A functional group is responsible for a compound's characteristic reactions.
List the kinds of bond present in propane and ask which of them makes it react characteristically.

items.stem: Ethanoic acid, $\ce{CH3COOH}$, and methyl methanoate, $\ce{HCOOCH3}$, both have molecular formula $\ce{C2H4O2}$. Deduce which statement about their boiling points is correct.

options.A: Ethanoic acid has the higher boiling point, because its carboxyl group allows hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
options.B: The two boiling points are the same, because the compounds have the same molecular formula.
options.C: Methyl methanoate has the higher boiling point, because its ester group allows hydrogen bonding between its own molecules.
options.D: Methyl methanoate has the higher boiling point, because it has the larger relative molecular mass.

items.explanation: Ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid and methyl methanoate is an ester. Both contain polar bonds, but only ethanoic acid has an O-H bond and can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules. These stronger intermolecular attractions give ethanoic acid the higher boiling point. A shared molecular formula does not imply identical physical properties, so the claim that the boiling points must be the same is wrong. Methyl methanoate has no O-H bond and cannot hydrogen-bond to itself, so the claim that its ester group allows hydrogen bonding between its own molecules is wrong. The two compounds have the same molecular formula and therefore the same relative molecular mass, so the claim that methyl methanoate has the larger relative molecular mass is wrong.
hints: Identify the carboxylic acid group and the ester group.
Compare the intermolecular forces in the two pure substances.
Which compound has a hydrogen atom bonded directly to oxygen and can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?

flashcards.back: A compound made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms only.

9701-13.1.1.motivate: You can recognise a hydrocarbon by checking its elements, regardless of its shape or size.
9701-13.1.1.establish: A hydrocarbon is a compound made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms only. A formula containing oxygen, nitrogen or a halogen is not a hydrocarbon, even if most atoms are carbon and hydrogen.
9701-13.1.1.connect: This definition identifies alkanes and alkenes as hydrocarbons, but excludes alcohols and carboxylic acids.
9701-13.1.1.note:
- Hydrocarbon: carbon and hydrogen atoms only.
- Any other element excludes the compound.
9701-13.1.1.self_explain: Why is ethanol not a hydrocarbon even though it contains carbon and hydrogen?
9701-13.1.1.plain_words: Start from neutral carbon making four covalent bonds: single, double and triple bonds contribute one, two and three to that total. A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen; shape and bond order do not decide membership.

terms.meaning: Compound whose only elements are carbon and hydrogen.
For the neutral carbon structures here, bond orders around each carbon total four.

forms.name: Classify hydrocarbons from complete formulas
wordings: Identify which compounds are hydrocarbons and justify each choice.
forms.example: Compare $\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{CH2=CH2}$ and $\ce{CH3OH}$. Step 1: list elements in each. Step 2: the first two contain C and H only, so qualify. Step 3: the third also contains O, so does not.
forms.check: Identify which of $\ce{CH3CH2CH3}$, $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$ and $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$ are hydrocarbons. Give an element-based reason for each decision.
forms.answer: The first and second are hydrocarbons because they contain only carbon and hydrogen. The third is not because it contains oxygen.

rubric.point: First and second qualify; third does not, with the only-C-and-H criterion and the oxygen exclusion.

misconceptions.idea: Any compound containing carbon and hydrogen is a hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.temptation: The formula begins with a carbon chain.
misconceptions.fix: Read every element symbol; an O, N or halogen excludes it.

9701-13.1.1.diagram_reason: This form assesses element membership; explicit structural formulas show all the needed information.
source_gaps: The reviewed sources establish these teaching forms; a complete audit of official question papers and mark schemes remains pending.

9701-13.1.2.motivate: A molecule can be organic without possessing a characteristic functional group.
9701-13.1.2.establish: Alkanes are simple, saturated hydrocarbons. They contain carbon and hydrogen only and have carbon–carbon single bonds. Alkanes have no functional group; their C–C and C–H bonds form the hydrocarbon framework rather than a distinctive group such as C=C or –OH.
9701-13.1.2.connect: Compare an alkane with an alkene: the alkene has a C=C functional group, which gives it characteristic addition reactions.
9701-13.1.2.note:
- Alkanes are simple hydrocarbons.
- Alkanes have no functional group.
- Saturated means carbon–carbon single bonds only.
9701-13.1.2.self_explain: Why does the presence of C–H bonds not make an alkane a functional-group compound?
9701-13.1.2.plain_words: Use two separate decisions: which elements are present, and whether there is a characteristic functional group. An alkane is a saturated hydrocarbon with no functional group; an alkene is a hydrocarbon with a carbon–carbon double bond.

terms.meaning: Saturated hydrocarbon with no functional group.
Contains only single carbon–carbon bonds.
Carbon–carbon double bond.

forms.name: Separate hydrocarbon membership from functional groups
wordings: Compare compounds as hydrocarbons and identify any functional group.
forms.example: For $\ce{CH3CH3}$, $\ce{CH2=CHCH3}$ and $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$: list their elements first. The first two are hydrocarbons. Then inspect bonds: the first is an alkane with no functional group; the second has C=C; the third is an alcohol with O–H and is not a hydrocarbon.
forms.check: For A $\ce{CH3(CH2)3CH3}$, B $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3}$ and C $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl}$, identify the alkane and state whether each is a hydrocarbon and whether each has a functional group.
forms.answer: A is the alkane: hydrocarbon, no functional group. B is a hydrocarbon with an alkene C=C group. C is not a hydrocarbon because of Cl; it is a halogenoalkane with a C–Cl group.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf pp.2–5; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

rubric.point: A: alkane, hydrocarbon, no functional group.
B: hydrocarbon with C=C functional group.
C: not a hydrocarbon; C–Cl functional group.

misconceptions.idea: All organic compounds must have functional groups.
misconceptions.temptation: Organic families are often introduced by their functional groups.
misconceptions.fix: Alkanes are the explicit exception; their ordinary C–C and C–H bonds do not count.

9701-13.1.2.diagram_reason: Connectivity is explicit in the formulas; a separate image would repeat it.
source_gaps: The reviewed sources establish these teaching forms; a complete audit of official question papers and mark schemes remains pending.

9701-13.1.3.motivate: Two compounds with similar carbon skeletons can react differently because one group changes.
9701-13.1.3.establish: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic chemical reactions. In the syllabus classes, the group dictates chemical properties and strongly influences physical properties. For example, an alkene contains C=C, an alcohol –OH, an aldehyde –CHO, a ketone an internal C=O, a carboxylic acid –COOH, and an ester –COO–. Halogenoalkanes, acyl chlorides, amines, amides and nitriles have their own identifying groups. Members of one homologous series share the same functional group and characteristic reactions.
9701-13.1.3.connect: First identify the group, then use the formulas and naming rules for that class.
9701-13.1.3.note:
- Functional groups give characteristic reactions.
- They influence physical and chemical properties.
- One homologous series shares one functional group.
9701-13.1.3.self_explain: Why do propene and propanol have different characteristic reactions?
9701-13.1.3.plain_words: Locate a group, then inspect its neighbours. The same carbonyl bond occurs in several classes. Functional groups explain characteristic chemical behaviour, while chain length and shape also affect physical properties.

terms.meaning: Atom or group responsible for characteristic chemical reactions.
Carbon double-bonded to oxygen; inspect adjoining atoms to classify it.
Aldehyde: carbonyl carbon bonded to H; ketone: carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbon atoms.
Acid: carbonyl carbon bonded to O–H. Ester: carbonyl carbon bonded to O–carbon.
Halogenoalkane: C–halogen; acyl chloride: carbonyl C–Cl; amine: nitrogen bonded to carbon without an adjacent carbonyl; amide: carbonyl C–N; nitrile: carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen.
terms.spoken: halogenoalkane; acyl chloride; amine; amide; nitrile

terms.meaning: Family sharing a functional group and general formula, with successive members differing by one methylene unit.

forms.name: Distinguish aldehydes and ketones by connectivity
wordings: Identify the carbonyl class from the atoms bonded to its carbonyl carbon.
forms.example: Compare $\ce{CH3CHO}$ with $\ce{CH3COCH3}$. First find C=O. In the first, its carbon also bonds to H: aldehyde. In the second, it bonds to two carbon atoms: ketone.
forms.check: Identify the functional-group classes in $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CHO}$ and $\ce{CH3CH2COCH2CH3}$. Explain using the neighbours of the carbonyl carbon.
forms.answer: The first is an aldehyde because its carbonyl carbon bonds to H. The second is a ketone because that carbon bonds to two carbon atoms.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf p.5; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

rubric.point: First: aldehyde, carbonyl carbon bonded to H.
Second: ketone, carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbons.

forms.name: Distinguish carboxylic acids and esters by connectivity
wordings: Identify the group using the atom beyond the single-bond oxygen.
forms.example: In $\ce{HCOOH}$, the single-bond oxygen bears H: carboxylic acid. In $\ce{HCOOCH3}$ it bears carbon: ester. The shared C=O alone cannot distinguish them.
forms.check: Identify and justify the functional-group classes of $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COOH}$ and $\ce{CH3CH2COOCH2CH3}$.
forms.answer: The first is a carboxylic acid: C(=O)–O–H. The second is an ester: C(=O)–O–C.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf p.5; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

rubric.point: First is an acid with carbonyl C bonded to O–H.
Second is an ester with carbonyl C bonded to O–carbon.

forms.name: Relate functional groups to characteristic properties
wordings: Explain a chemical similarity and a limit on physical-property predictions.
forms.example: Ethanol and propan-1-ol both contain an alcohol group, so they show characteristic alcohol chemistry. Their different chain lengths mean their boiling points need not match: the group does not determine every physical value alone.
forms.check: Butan-1-ol and pentan-1-ol both have an alcohol group. Explain why they can show similar characteristic chemical reactions and why their boiling points need not be identical. No reaction equation or numerical value is required.
forms.answer: The shared alcohol functional group accounts for characteristic alcohol reactions. Chain length also affects intermolecular attractions, so sharing a group does not require identical boiling points.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf pp.2,4–5; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

rubric.point: Shared functional group gives characteristic chemical behaviour.
Different chain lengths can change intermolecular attractions and physical properties.

misconceptions.idea: A carbonyl bond always means ketone.
misconceptions.temptation: C=O is the most noticeable part of several groups.
misconceptions.fix: Inspect all attachments to the carbonyl carbon before naming the group.

9701-13.1.3.diagram_reason: Unambiguous condensed formulas display the distinguishing connectivity; no new source graphic was requested.

9701-13.1.4.motivate: One molecule can be represented in four ways; each representation answers a different question.
9701-13.1.4.establish: A general formula expresses the composition of a homologous series using $n$, such as $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ for acyclic alkanes. A structural formula shows atom and group connectivity in condensed form. A displayed formula shows every atom and every bond, including O–H. A skeletal formula shows the carbon framework as lines: each unlabelled end or vertex is carbon, and carbon-bound hydrogens are omitted. Infer them by giving each carbon four bonds. Show heteroatoms and hydrogens on them. Interpret and use these representations for the syllabus classes, including hydrocarbons, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, carbonyl compounds, acids, esters, acyl chlorides, amines, amides and nitriles.
9701-13.1.4.connect: Count skeletal atoms and complete valencies before deducing a molecular formula.
9701-13.1.4.note:
- General formula: series composition using $n$.
- Structural formula: condensed connectivity.
- Displayed formula: all atoms and bonds.
- Skeletal formula: carbon at each unlabelled end and vertex.
9701-13.1.4.self_explain: What must you add mentally when reading a skeletal formula?
9701-13.1.4.plain_words: First decide what information the representation must show. A general formula covers a family; a structural formula fixes connectivity; a displayed formula includes every bond. In a skeletal formula, count unlabelled ends and vertices and restore hydrogen using bond orders.

terms.meaning: Composition pattern for a stated homologous series.
terms.spoken: C n H two n plus two

terms.meaning: Conventional groups arranged to specify one unambiguous connectivity.
terms.spoken: C H three C H two C H two O H

terms.meaning: Every atom and bond is shown, including bonds to hydrogen.
Unlabelled ends and vertices are C; infer carbon-bound H; label heteroatoms and their H.

forms.name: Use a general formula within its stated scope
wordings: Deduce the molecular formula of a member of a specified series.
forms.example: An acyclic saturated alkane has general formula $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$. For three carbons, substitute n=3, giving H=8 and $\ce{C3H8}$. This relation assumes no ring and no multiple bond.
forms.check: Deduce the molecular formula of an acyclic saturated alkane with six carbon atoms, using its general formula.

rubric.point: Six carbons and fourteen hydrogens from the alkane relation.

forms.name: Write an unambiguous structural formula
wordings: Give a structural formula that locates the functional group.
forms.example: For propan-1-ol, write $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$: the order of groups places O–H on the terminal carbon. A formula giving only totals cannot distinguish different alcohol connectivities.
forms.check: Give an unambiguous condensed structural formula of pentan-2-ol.
forms.answer: $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3}$; the reversed equivalent $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH(OH)CH3}$ is equally valid.

rubric.point: Five-carbon chain with O–H attached to carbon 2; accept reversed or other unambiguous equivalent structural notation.

forms.name: Expand a structural formula to a displayed formula
wordings: Draw every atom and bond, including O–H.
forms.example: Expand $\ce{CH3OH}$ by drawing C–O–H, then attach three separately drawn H atoms to carbon by three single bonds. Carbon has four bonds, oxygen two, and every H one. The O–H line must be present; an OH label alone is not fully displayed.
forms.check: Draw the fully displayed formula of $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$, including every bond to hydrogen.
forms.answer: Draw a three-carbon single-bond chain ending C–O–H. Attach three separate H atoms to the opposite terminal C and two separate H atoms to each other C. Show seven C–H bonds, two C–C bonds, one C–O bond and one O–H bond; accept any orientation.
forms.source: Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf; ER 9701 s19 P22 Q5

rubric.point: Correct three-carbon chain and C–O–H connectivity, with all bonds single.
All eight H atoms and all bonds shown explicitly, including seven C–H and one O–H.

forms.name: Interpret skeletal ends, vertices and bond orders
wordings: Recover a structural formula from an explicitly described skeletal structure.
forms.example: A skeletal chain has three unlabelled carbon positions joined C=C–C, with O–H bonded to the last carbon. The carbon bond-order totals are 2, 3 and 2, so add 2, 1 and 2 carbon-bound H respectively. The structural formula is $\ce{CH2=CHCH2OH}$; the shown O–H contributes another H.
forms.check: A skeletal chain has four unlabelled carbon positions in sequence: two ends and two vertices, labelled here A–B–C–D only to identify positions. A–B and C–D are single bonds, B=C is double, and D is single-bonded to a labelled O–H group. Deduce an unambiguous condensed structural formula. State the hydrogen count at each carbon position and at oxygen.
forms.answer: $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH2OH}$, or the reversed equivalent. A, B, C and D carry 3, 1, 1 and 2 H atoms respectively; O bears the shown H.

rubric.point: Four-carbon connectivity with central C=C and terminal C–O–H.
Carbon hydrogen counts 3,1,1,2 and the explicitly shown hydroxyl hydrogen.

misconceptions.idea: Skeletal formulas write all carbon and hydrogen atoms explicitly.
misconceptions.fix: Include every unlabelled end and vertex, then supply H from valency four.

9701-13.1.5.motivate: A systematic name lets someone reconstruct a molecule's connectivity.
9701-13.1.5.establish: For simple aliphatic molecules up to six carbons, choose the longest parent chain containing the principal functional group. Number it to give that group the lowest locant. Use a carbon stem from meth- through hex-, indicate substituents and their positions, and give the class suffix, for example propan-2-ol or butanoic acid. Include a nitrile carbon in the parent count. For straight-chain esters $\ce{RCOOR'}$, name the O-bonded alkyl $\ce{R'}$ first and the acid-derived alkanoate part second; up to six carbons may occur in each ester part. This syllabus restricts esters and nitriles to straight chains.
9701-13.1.5.connect: The functional group identified first determines the suffix and often controls numbering.
9701-13.1.5.note:
- Choose the parent chain containing the main group.
- Number for the lowest functional-group locant.
- Ester: O-bonded alkyl name, then alkanoate.
- Count nitrile carbon in its parent chain.
9701-13.1.5.self_explain: Which part of methyl propanoate supplies the word methyl?
9701-13.1.5.plain_words: Choose a parent containing the principal group and number for that group before locating branches. For esters split the O-bonded alkyl from the acid-derived chain. For nitriles include the carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen in the parent count.

terms.meaning: Longest eligible continuous carbon chain containing the principal group.
terms.notation: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-

terms.meaning: Number identifying the position of a group or multiple bond.
Alkyl from the single-bond oxygen side, then alkanoate from the carbonyl side.
terms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf p.12; ER 9701 s19 P22 Q5

terms.meaning: The carbon in the nitrile group is carbon 1 of the parent.

forms.name: Choose and number a branched parent with a functional group
wordings: Name a branched alcohol, selecting its parent and numbering.
forms.example: Name $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2OH}$. Step 1: the longest chain containing the O–H-bearing carbon has four carbons. Step 2: number from that end to put OH at 1. Step 3: methyl is at 2. Combine: 2-methylbutan-1-ol.
forms.check: Name $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CH(CH3)CH3}$. State the parent-chain length and the locants of OH and the methyl branch.
forms.answer: The five-carbon parent is numbered for OH at 2 rather than 4; methyl is at 4. The name is 4-methylpentan-2-ol.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf pp.8–13; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

rubric.point: Five-carbon parent numbered with OH at 2 and methyl at 4.
Correct full systematic name: 4-methylpentan-2-ol.

forms.name: Name a straight-chain ester by separating its two parts
wordings: Name an ester and identify which carbon atoms supply each name part.
forms.example: For $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COOCH3}$, separate the single-bond oxygen from the carbonyl side. O bonds to a one-carbon methyl group. The acid-derived chain has four carbons including C=O, giving butanoate. Combine: methyl butanoate.
forms.check: Name $\ce{CH3COOCH2CH2CH3}$. State the number of carbon atoms in the O-bonded alkyl part and in the acid-derived part.
forms.answer: Propyl ethanoate. The O-bonded alkyl has three carbons; the acid-derived part has two including the carbonyl carbon.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf p.12; ER 9701 s19 P22 Q5

rubric.point: The O-bonded fragment has three carbons and is propyl.
The acid-derived fragment has two carbons including the carbonyl carbon and is ethanoate; the full name is propyl ethanoate.

forms.name: Count the nitrile carbon when naming a straight chain
wordings: Name a nitrile using the complete parent count.
forms.example: For $\ce{CH3CH2C#N}$, the alkyl fragment has two carbons but the nitrile adds a third. Count that carbon as 1 and use the three-carbon stem: propanenitrile.
forms.check: Name $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2C#N}$ and state how many carbon atoms are in the parent chain.
forms.answer: Pentanenitrile; five carbons including the nitrile carbon.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf p.12; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf

rubric.point: Five-carbon parent includes the nitrile carbon.
Correct name pentanenitrile.

misconceptions.idea: The carbonyl carbon belongs to the ester alkyl part.
misconceptions.temptation: The whole formula is counted as one chain.
misconceptions.fix: Find C(=O)–O first; name the group beyond O as alkyl and count C=O in the alkanoate.

misconceptions.idea: The nitrile carbon does not count in the parent.
misconceptions.temptation: Only the alkyl fragment is visibly repeated as CH groups.
misconceptions.fix: Count the carbon bonded to nitrogen as carbon 1.

9701-13.1.6.motivate: A drawing tells you the actual atom count; a simplest ratio may hide that count.
9701-13.1.6.establish: Deduce a molecular formula by counting all atoms in a structural or displayed formula. In a skeletal formula, count every unlabelled end and vertex as carbon, then supply carbon-bound hydrogens to complete carbon valency four, accounting for double or triple bonds. Include shown heteroatoms and their hydrogens. The molecular formula records actual numbers of atoms. The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio: divide all molecular subscripts by their greatest common factor. For $\ce{C4H8O2}$ this gives $\ce{C2H4O}$.
9701-13.1.6.connect: A correct skeletal count is the input for both formulas; only the empirical formula is reduced.
9701-13.1.6.note:
- Molecular formula: actual atom counts.
- Complete skeletal carbon valencies before counting H.
- Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio.
9701-13.1.6.self_explain: Why is $\ce{C2H4O}$ empirical but not molecular for methyl ethanoate?
9701-13.1.6.plain_words: Recover actual atom totals before simplifying anything. For a skeletal structure use bond orders to complete carbon valency and include shown O–H or N–H hydrogens. Only the empirical formula reduces every element count by the same greatest common divisor.

terms.meaning: Actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
terms.spoken: C six H twelve O two

terms.meaning: Simplest whole-number ratio of all element counts.
A number dividing every atom count, including implicit subscripts of one.

forms.name: Count molecular atoms including hidden and heteroatom hydrogens
wordings: Deduce a molecular formula from structural or skeletal connectivity.
forms.example: For $\ce{HOCH2CH2CH2OH}$, count C=3 and O=2. Each carbon has two C-bound H, so six; add one H on each oxygen to obtain H=8. The molecular formula is $\ce{C3H8O2}$. For a skeletal version of this same connectivity, the three carbon positions must also be counted before restoring H.
forms.check: A skeletal open chain has six unlabelled carbon positions in order, two ends and four vertices, with all C–C bonds single. Each terminal carbon is also single-bonded to one explicitly shown O–H group. Deduce its molecular formula. Account separately for carbon-bound H and oxygen-bound H.
forms.answer: $\ce{C6H14O2}$. Each terminal carbon is CH2 because it bonds to one C and one O; the four internal carbons are also CH2. There are twelve C-bound H and two O-bound H, giving fourteen H total.
forms.source: Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf; SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c13.1.pdf pp.6–7

rubric.point: Six carbon atoms and two oxygen atoms.
Twelve carbon-bound plus two oxygen-bound hydrogen atoms.
Molecular formula C6H14O2; equivalent atom-count reasoning accepted.

forms.name: Reduce every molecular subscript to an empirical formula
wordings: Deduce molecular and empirical formulas from an unambiguous structure.
forms.example: For $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COOH}$, count C=4, H=3+2+2+1=8 and O=2. Molecular formula: $\ce{C4H8O2}$. The common divisor of 4,8,2 is 2; empirical formula: $\ce{C2H4O}$. The molecular formula stays unreduced.
forms.check: Deduce both the molecular and empirical formulas of $\ce{HOCH2CH2CH2CH2OH}$. Show the common factor used.
forms.answer: C=4; H=8 on carbon plus 2 on oxygen; O=2. Molecular formula $\ce{C4H10O2}$. Divide every count by 2: empirical formula $\ce{C2H5O}$.
forms.source: Cambridge 9701 syllabus 2025–2027, pp.29–30, 78; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf; ER 9701 s22 P21 Q4

rubric.point: Actual totals give molecular formula C4H10O2.
Common factor two applied to all elements gives empirical formula C2H5O.

misconceptions.idea: The simplest ratio always gives the actual molecular formula.
misconceptions.temptation: Reducing numbers seems like a final step for every formula.
misconceptions.fix: Keep the counted molecular formula; reduce only the empirical formula.
